chunk_findings.detail: The attribute line `*/schema.json -diff linguist-vendored` (and `LICENSE -diff`) sets only `-diff`; it does not set `-text`. `-diff` merely tells diff to treat the path as binary — it leaves the `text` attribute *unspecified*, so git still auto-detects these JSON/LICENSE files as text and applies end-of-line conversion on checkout. On a Windows clone with the Git for Windows default `core.autocrlf=true` (or any `core.eol=crlf` configuration), git rewrites LF to CRLF in the working tree, so the bytes on disk are not the bytes in the blob. The manifest hashes and `tests/test_mcp_protocol_conformance.py` hash the on-disk files, so the sha256 comparison fails for all five revisions even though nothing upstream changed — the exact guarantee the file's own comment claims ("byte for byte, held to their sha256"). To actually hold that guarantee the pattern needs `-text` (i.e. `binary` / `-diff -merge -text`), not just `-diff`.

chunk_findings.detail: The "forged" token is produced by rewriting the last two characters of the genuine tag to `"AA"`. When the genuine tag already ends in `AA` (a hex digest under a random per-process key hits this about once in 256 runs; base64url similar order of magnitude), `forged` is byte-identical to `token`. The server then correctly serves the real state, `srv.handle(_retry(params, forged))` returns a *result*, and `reply["error"]["code"]` raises `KeyError` inside `assert reply["error"]["code"] == -32602`. So this merge-gating conformance test fails spuriously for a state that is not forged at all. The same construction is used for no other property (format, separator, length), so the "tampered token is refused" contract is only exercised on the branch where the mutation happens to change something. A deterministic mutation (e.g. flip the first tag character to a different symbol, or assert `forged != token` before presenting it) is needed for the test to be reliable.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_protocol_conformance.py `forged = f"{body}.{tag[:-2]}AA"` (in `test_a_state_this_server_did_not_issue_is_refused`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test's stated purpose is that the retry is "verified" and that "the server answers the retry like any modern call", but the only check on the server's handling is `check_reply(rev, "tools/call", M.Server(repo, agent="conformance").handle(retry))`, and `check_reply` also accepts an *error* envelope (it validates `JSONRPCErrorResponse` and returns). Concretely: if the freshly constructed `M.Server` refused the state (e.g. a state key not shared with the process that called `P.input_required`, or a binding on agent/tool that the retry fails), `handle` would return `{"error": {"code": -32602, ...}}`, the reply would still conform to the schema, and this test would pass while claiming the retry was served. The genuinely-issued-token acceptance is only asserted in `test_a_state_this_server_did_not_issue_is_refused` (`assert "result" in srv.handle(_retry(params, token))`), so the end-to-end MRTR path through a server that did not issue the state is not actually pinned by the test that names it.

chunk_findings.detail: `round_trip` treats "MAC verifies" as "payload is a well-formed state": after `hmac.compare_digest(mac, _mac(raw))` it does `payload = json.loads(raw)` and then `payload["b"]`, `payload["x"]`, `payload["s"]` with no type check. The MAC-valid preimages are not secret in the way the code assumes: the token handed to the client is `_b64(raw) + "." + _b64(_mac(raw))`, and `raw` contains `"b": _b64(_mac(binding_bytes))`, so the client learns the MAC *of the binding preimage* `X = json.dumps([method, {"arguments":…, "name":…, "uri":…}, who], sort_keys=True, separators=(",",":"), default=str)` — and it knows `X` exactly, because every field in it is taken from the request the client itself sent. So after any legitimate `InputRequiredResult` (e.g. a `tools/call` that asked for elicitation), the client can send the retry `requestState = _b64(X) + "." + <the `b` value from its own decoded token>`. In `round_trip`: `token.count(".") == 1` ✓, `_unb64(body)` decodes to `X`, `_unb64(tag)` equals `_mac(X)` so `compare_digest` **passes** ✓, and then `json.loads(X)` is a JSON *array*, so `payload["b"]` raises `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str`. `modern_check` wraps `round_trip` in `try: … except ValueError as exc`, and `TypeError` is not a `ValueError`, so the exception escapes `modern_check` and any caller that only distinguishes the documented `str | dict | None` returns; on a single-process stdio loop without a blanket `except`, that is a repeatable crash triggered by one malformed retry (and, at minimum, a non-JSON-RPC error/no reply for that `id`). The fix is either to validate the decoded payload inside `round_trip` (`isinstance(payload, dict)` and required keys, `isinstance(payload["x"], int)`, catching `TypeError`/`KeyError`) and raise `ValueError`, or to widen `modern_check`'s handler to `except (ValueError, TypeError, KeyError)`.

chunk_findings.detail: The rule `*/schema.json -diff linguist-vendored` clears only the diff attribute, so git's end-of-line handling for these vendored files is left to `core.autocrlf` / any higher-level `* text=auto`. `-diff` does not imply `-text` (the standard `binary` macro is `-diff -merge -text`), and the schemas are plain text JSON, so on any checkout where `core.autocrlf=true` (the default for Git for Windows) or where a root `.gitattributes` sets `text=auto`, git writes `2024-11-05/schema.json` (and the other four) out with CRLF even though the blob and the manifest hash are LF. Concretely: a Windows contributor clones, `git status` is clean, but `tests/test_mcp_protocol_conformance.py` computes `sha256` over the CRLF bytes, gets a value different from `61cea239...` in `manifest.json`, and fails — exactly the "byte for byte" property line 1 of this same file claims is enforced. The fix is to use `binary`/`-text` on these paths so checkout never rewrites them.

data.summary: mcp_protocol.input_required seals requestState as b64(raw).b64(mac(raw)) where raw carries b = mac(binding preimage X), and X is built only from what the client sent. Both MACs use one key with no domain separation, so a client presents b64(X).b64(b): the MAC verifies, json.loads(X) is a list, payload['b'] raises TypeError, which modern_check does not catch (it catches ValueError) -- an uncaught exception instead of -32602. Found by the critic review (lan-deepseek-v4.1-flash) on the unmerged branch.

data.body: B-onboard-harness built enable_project_servers, copy_local_configs and install_shell_command (tested) but B-onboard-surface wired no stage to them, so the onboard prompt's stage 2 (onboard.md: enabledMcpjsonServers, 'the shell must reach the same ddflow', 'a sibling project ... ask before copying') still teaches the hand-work. chunk_findings.detail:
The stated intent for this change is to "delete truly dead helpers (`harness.enable_project_servers`, `copy_local_configs`, `install_shell_command`, `adopt._own_distribution`, `context._resolved`, `_dedupe.with_check`, `cli.py:134/319`)" and to keep in the allowlist only things with a *recorded planned caller* (`flowcontrol`, `flowsignals`, `quota`). The diff instead adds the three harness helpers to `KEPT_UNREFERENCED`:

```
"ddflow/services/harness.py:enable_project_servers": "B-hx-onboard-generic",
"ddflow/services/harness.py:copy_local_configs": "B-onboard-harness-stage",
"ddflow/services/harness.py:install_shell_command": "B-onboard-harness-stage",
```

Concretely: `_unreferenced_functions()` runs `_unreferenced(...)` and then drops anything whose `_kept_key` is in `KEPT_UNREFERENCED`. For a module-level `enable_project_servers` at `ddflow/services/harness.py:41`, `_kept_key("ddflow/services/harness.py:41 enable_project_servers")` yields exactly `"ddflow/services/harness.py:enable_project_servers"`, so it is filtered out regardless of whether the function was deleted in the rest of the change. The baseline `"unreferenced_functions": 6` is therefore unchanged whether those three functions exist or not, and the vulture ratchet that this change introduces will never surface them. So the step the intent describes — deleting these three truly-dead helpers — is neither performed nor detectable by the new guard; if they were in fact deleted in another part of the change, these entries are stale and the "an entry leaves this list in the change that gives it a caller" rule is violated for them (they left by deletion, not by getting a caller). Either way the allowlist and the stated intent cannot both be satisfied: the three names the change says it removes are the three it whitelists.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own stated intent is to *delete* the truly dead helpers `harness.enable_project_servers`, `harness.copy_local_configs` and `harness.install_shell_command`, but the diff instead adds exactly those three symbols to `KEPT_UNREFERENCED` ("B-hx-onboard-generic" / "B-onboard-harness-stage"). Because `_unreferenced_functions()` filters out every name whose `_kept_key` is in that dict, those three are never returned and the new dead-code ratchet can never flag them: the dead code is enshrined as "kept" for as long as the entry lives. This also makes the new baseline inconsistent. The intent enumerates exactly six module-level, single-underscore/plain dead functions to remove (`harness.enable_project_servers`, `copy_local_configs`, `install_shell_command`, `adopt._own_distribution`, `context._resolved`, `_dedupe.with_check`) — which is exactly the value committed as `"unreferenced_functions": 6`. Since three of those six are now filtered out by `KEPT_UNREFERENCED`, `_unreferenced_functions()` can return at most the remaining three (and 0 once the intended deletion of `_own_distribution`/`_resolved`/`with_check` happens elsewhere in this change), so the guard either fails against its own baseline (6 vs 3/0) or silently tolerates three functions the change was written to delete. Either way the allowlist entry, not the backlog, is what is suppressing them.
